topic.name: Using Differentiation to Calculate Critical Points

question.text: What are the critical points of the function $f(x) = \dfrac {x }{x^2 + 4}?$
question.explanation:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} \left( \dfrac {x }{x^2 + 4} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{(x)' \cdot (x^2+4) - x \cdot (x^2+4)'}{(x^2+4)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {(x^2 + 4) - x \cdot 2x}{(x^2 + 4)^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4-x^2}{(x^2 + 4)^2}. \end{align*}

We now proceed to find the critical points:

  • First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \dfrac{4-x^2}{(x^2 + 4)^2} &= 0 \\[5pt] 4-x^2&= 0 \\[5pt] x^2&= 4 \\[5pt] x &= \pm 2. \end{align*} Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

  • Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

question.text: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)=e^{x^3-3x}.$
question.explanation:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} \left(e^{x^3-3x}\right) \\[5pt] &= \left(x^3-3x\right)'e^{x^3-3x}\\[5pt] &=(3x^2-3)e^{x^3-3x}. \end{align*}

We now proceed to find the critical points:

  • First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} (3x^2-3)e^{x^3-3x} &=0\\[5pt] \end{align*} Since $e^{x^3-3x} \neq 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by $e^{x^3-3x}$ and solve the resulting equation. \begin{align*} 3x^2-3&=0\\[5pt] 3(x^2-1) &= 0\\[5pt] 3(x-1)(x+1) &= 0\\[5pt] x &= -1,\, 1 \end{align*} Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x = 1$ and $x=-1.$

  • Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=-1.$

example.title: Finding Critical Points of Exponential Functions

question.text: Consider the function $f(x) = 3\sin{x} + 2\cos{x}.$ If the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x \in (0, 2\pi)$ are $x = x_1$ and $x = x_2,$ what is the value of $x_1 \cdot x_2?$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
question.explanation:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x = c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain \begin{align*} f'(x) & = \dfrac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x} \left( 3\sin{x} + 2\cos{x} \right) \\[5pt] & = 3\cos{x} + 2(-\sin{x})\\[5pt] & = 3\cos{x} - 2\sin{x}. \end{align*}

We now proceed to find the critical points:

  • First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} 3\cos{x} - 2\sin{x} & = 0\\[5pt] 2\sin{x} & = 3\cos{x}\\[5pt] \dfrac{\sin{x}}{\cos{x}} & = \dfrac{3}{2} \cdot \dfrac{\cos{x}}{\cos{x}}\\[5pt] \tan{x} & = \dfrac{3}{2} \end{align*} The general solution to our equation is \begin{align*} x & = \arctan\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) + n\pi. \end{align*} We set $n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0 \lt x \lt 2\pi.$

    • setting $n = 0$ gives $x \approx 0.982\,79$ rounded to five decimal places

    • setting $n = 1$ gives $x \approx 4.124\,39$ rounded to five decimal places

    All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0 \lt x \lt 2\pi.$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x \in (0, 2\pi)$ are \[ x \approx 0.982\,79 , \qquad x \approx 4.124\,39. \] Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x \approx 0.982\,79$ and $x \approx 4.124\,39.$

  • Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x \in (0,2\pi).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x \in (0,2\pi)$ are $x_1 \approx 0.982\,79$ and $x_2 \approx 4.124\,39.$

Finally, \[ x_1 \cdot x_2 \approx 0.982\,79 \cdot 4.124\,39 \approx 4.05 \] rounded to two decimal places
